anchors.fact: With Repeal coming in 1933, the *New York Sun* gave G. Selmer Fougner a series to help readers find their way around legal wine and spirits, which were unfamiliar to them. His daily column began on 20 October 1933 and ran until he died in 1941 (Oxford pdf 833; F4).
anchors.meaning: He didn't make a speech. He made a thing that came out daily, with his name on it, and he kept it up.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: they argue in what they make, not across the table; fear: going quiet when it matters (answered by the record, never claimed of him)

anchors.fact: Before him, wine writing tended to be high-toned and mystifying, and cocktail writing jocular and even aggressively vulgar. Oxford: "Fougner was neither." He didn't talk down to people who drank cocktails or beer (pdf 833; F6, F8).
anchors.meaning: The belief is shown in how the thing is made. Never "he didn't argue": he did, in print, "gently (usually)" (pdf 834; F11, G3).
anchors.speaksTo: Leave a mark; the made thing *is* the argument

anchors.fact: He answered readers' questions patiently, however silly: one asked whether all scotch was made in Australia (pdf 833; F9). Not "every" question.
anchors.meaning: Nobody gets talked down to: that's what the guest's made things give. The humour is the reader's question, not Fougner's wit (F7).
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: nobody talked down to

anchors.fact: When he didn't know an answer, he put the question to his readers, nationwide. Many of them had first-hand knowledge of how famous drinks began, and the column "seems to have been" especially popular with former bartenders. Their testimony still lights up the history of famous drinks, the Ward Eight among them (pdf 833–834; F10).
anchors.meaning: The made thing lets other people say what they know, together. It's a door he opened, never a man stuck for an answer (that's the Problem Solver's ground).
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: others get words and room to join in

anchors.fact: In 1934, while Fougner was seeking more about the Ward Eight, a reader sent the *Sun* a recipe: a whisky sour made to fix "certain objectionable features" of it, with bourbon, grenadine, orange bitters or (as "many prefer") half an orange's juice, plain water or seltzer, in a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass over "a rather large piece of ice". Fresh mint, when there was any, went in place of crème de menthe, bruised and added with the orange slices ("This is an improvement"). Wondrich prints this letter rather than the only pre-Prohibition recipe, then gives his own build with rye (*Imbibe!* pdf 243–244; W1–W5).
anchors.meaning: The recipe exists because the column asked and someone answered: the made thing still working decades later. Never "the original Ward Eight" (the origin is legend, W8), and never "the books don't print it" (Wondrich prints the letter).
anchors.speaksTo: the made thing carried beyond him

anchors.fact: Spec v1: 75 ml bourbon (40–46%), 30 lemon, 30 orange (half an orange), 15 ml grenadine of pomegranate juice and sugar only, short-shaken for about 5 s (*Codex* p. 138's Collins method), over one large piece of ice in a heavy round-bowled beer glass, topped with 45 ml seltzer, then the mint (bruised), orange half-slices, pineapple and a cherry. **The letter's:** bourbon, lemon, orange juice, grenadine, seltzer, the ice, the glass, the mint and the fruit (pdf 243–244). **Ours:** the shake (the reader built it in the glass), the measures (the letter gives none that convert: "three-quarters full" of a whisky glass), a fixed grenadine dose, and the sugar left out.
anchors.meaning: Every ingredient comes from someone who wrote to the column, or from Fougner. Only the method and the measures are the bartender's. Never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: the made thing carried beyond him; brought others in

anchors.fact: The reader: "The amount of sugar should be regulated to taste, and likewise the grenadine" (pdf 244). Spec v1 leaves his barspoon out, and the orange and grenadine carry the sweetness (balance.py: with the spoon it's 8.00 g, OUT).
anchors.meaning: The letter left room for the drinker, so the drinker's choice is on the page. Say "his letter leaves the sugar to taste", never "he said to leave it out".

anchors.fact: In June 1936, after Repeal, when American commercial grenadine was imitation, Fougner wrote of "innumerable products masquerading under that name" and claimed the reputable French makers used real pomegranate juice. Oxford: it "took some decades to sink in" (pdf 947–948; G2–G4). Grenadine was in the Ward Eight from the start (pdf 2120). He gave no home recipe (G3).
anchors.meaning: Where he did argue, he argued in the column, and the point landed slowly. No cause claimed. Our syrup is our choice, tied to his line, never "as he made it", never "fakes", never "the argument", never "my own pomegranate syrup" (*Till Spring*).
anchors.speaksTo: put the finished thing out; it lands later

anchors.fact: *Flavor Matrix* pdf 200: pomegranate is "mostly fruity" but "also characterized by sharper aromas such as anise and mint". Mint isn't on its pairings list, and the page describes the fruit and its juice, not a syrup.
anchors.kind: pairing (Checks only; one clause in y4)
anchors.meaning: The reader's 1934 mint and Fougner's 1936 pomegranate share an aroma. Wording: "pomegranate has a note of mint of its own" or "pomegranate's own aromas include mint". Never "hint" or "faint" (strength words the page doesn't give; "hint" was my own r3 shorthand, struck), and never "the Matrix pairs them".

anchors.fact: The reader adds the mint "with the slices of orange, &c.", after the glass is filled (pdf 244): last.
anchors.meaning: "Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it" is on the page. "Wrote", not "did".

cocktail.closingLine: Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it. Then see who writes back.
cocktail.glassware: a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass (about 400 ml), with one large piece of ice
method: Make the grenadine ahead. Put the pomegranate juice and sugar in a jar, close it and shake (or blend) until the sugar has dissolved. Keep it in the fridge.
Put one large piece of ice in a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass.
Pour the bourbon, lemon juice, orange juice and grenadine into a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake briefly, about five seconds. That leaves room for the seltzer.
Strain it into the glass, over the ice.
Top up with the cold seltzer (soda water).
Press the mint sprig once between your fingers to wake it up. Tuck it into the glass with the orange half-slices, the pineapple and the cherry, the way the reader wrote it.
cocktail.name: The Long Answer

recipe.note: the reader's own choice, where the older recipes say rye
the reader said many preferred it to orange bitters
real pomegranate, which Fougner wrote the reputable French makers used
the reader wrote "plain water or seltzer"; I chose the seltzer
his "improvement", in place of crème de menthe

recipe.item: fresh cherry, or a cherry kept in brandy (not a bright-red maraschino-style one)
*for the grenadine:* 250 g pure pomegranate juice (unsweetened; a bottle is fine) and 250 g sugar
recipe.note: nothing else: no orange, no acids

cocktail.tagline: What you make gives people the words they were missing.

reading.epigraph: This glass starts from a reader's letter to a New York paper, in 1934.
whoYouAre: When something matters to you and the arguing starts, you're rarely the loudest person there. Often you go quiet. The right words turn up later, on the way home, and you can lose sleep over the ones you didn't say. Losing an argument, you get over. Staying quiet when it really mattered, you don't.

Then you make something: a page, a song, a picture, a menu, a message that took all evening. In that, you say all of it, plainly, and you mean every word. Sometimes you wonder whether making things instead of arguing is just a nicer way of hiding. It isn't. An argument changes one mind, if you're lucky. What you make travels. It gives people the words they were missing, and room to join in without anyone being talked down to. That's your way of standing up for something, and it brings people together.
yours: In the autumn of 1933, with Prohibition about to end, the *Sun*, a New York newspaper, gave a writer named G. Selmer Fougner a daily series to help its readers find their way around legal wine and spirits. Wine writing then tended to be grand and mystifying, and cocktail writing jokey, even crude. Fougner was neither. He didn't talk down to anyone who liked a cocktail or a beer, and he answered readers' questions patiently, however silly. One wanted to know whether all scotch was really made in Australia.

When he had a view, he gave it, gently, usually. In 1936, when the grenadine sold in America was mostly imitation, he wrote that the reputable French makers used real pomegranate. And when he didn't know an answer, he put the question to readers all over the country, many of whom had been there when famous drinks began, and they wrote back. The column ran daily until he died in 1941.

This was his way of standing up for something, I like to think: not with a speech, but with a daily column, where nobody was laughed at for asking and anyone who knew better could say so. It's your way too. And look at what came back when he asked. More than one reader wrote to him about a single Boston drink, and one of those letters holds the recipe behind the cocktail I've made for you.

It's the Ward Eight, Boston's best-known cocktail, built from that reader's 1934 recipe: bourbon, lemon, grenadine and half an orange, squeezed, which he said many people preferred, over a rather large piece of ice in a heavy, round-bowled glass "of the type generally used for beer". Fresh mint goes in with the orange slices, pineapple and cherry he listed, in place of a mint liqueur. "This is an improvement," the reader wrote. He allowed plain water or seltzer; I chose the seltzer. His letter leaves the sugar to taste, so I left out the spoon, because the orange and the grenadine carry the sweetness. The grenadine is made from real pomegranate, for Fougner's column of 1936. Pomegranate's own aromas include mint, so the reader's improvement and the columnist's point share a scent. It's long, bright and tart, a hazy rosy orange, and strong: the reader called his "highly potent".

Somewhere there's a thing you made about what you believe, and never put out: the page, the song, the long message sitting in drafts. It's ready. But sending it is the argument, so it waits. Send it, where anyone can see it. Then ask people what they think, and mean the question. Some of the answers will surprise you, and you'll find you were never standing up for it alone.
